questions.question: For absolutely continuous losses with normalised densities, $f_X-f_Y$ is non-negative before a threshold and non-positive afterwards. Which CDF comparison follows for every real $t$?
options: $F_X(t)\le F_Y(t)$.
$F_X(t)=F_Y(t)$ necessarily.
$F_X(t)\ge F_Y(t)$.
$F_X(t)-F_Y(t)=f_X(t)-f_Y(t)$.

questions.question: Two normalised densities have difference $d=f_X-f_Y$, non-negative below a threshold and non-positive above it. Why can their CDF difference $D(t)=F_X(t)-F_Y(t)$ not become negative after that threshold?
options: The remaining tail satisfies $D(t)=-\int_t^\infty d(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\ge0$.
The density difference must remain non-negative there.
The CDF difference equals the pointwise value of d.
The later density values no longer affect either CDF.

questions.question: For continuous density versions, define $d(t)=f_X(t)-f_Y(t)$ and $D(t)=F_X(t)-F_Y(t)$. At a point where both CDFs are differentiable, what does $d(t)<0$ tell us directly?
options: $D(t)<0$, regardless of earlier mass.
$D'(t)<0$, not necessarily $D(t)<0$.
$D(t)=0$ because the densities have crossed.
$D'(t)>0$ because CDFs increase.

questions.question: A single-crossing criterion uses weak inequalities: $f_X-f_Y\ge0$ below a threshold and $\le0$ above it. The two densities coincide on an interval around a valid threshold. Must that threshold be unique?
options: Yes; equality at more than one point destroys the criterion.
Yes; the threshold must be an atom of both laws.
No; weak signs reverse the resulting CDF order.
No; any suitable point in that equality interval may work.

questions.question: Two normalised density versions satisfy the single-crossing signs almost everywhere. One density value is changed at one isolated point while it remains non-negative. What happens to the CDF comparison established by the criterion?
options: It reverses at the altered threshold.
It gains a point mass at the altered value.
It remains unchanged because the altered set has zero length.
It changes the mean whenever the new height is larger.

questions.question: On $(0,1)$, losses have density versions $f_X(t)=2(1-t)$ and $f_Y(t)=2t$, both zero elsewhere. At what point does their difference change from positive to negative?
On $(0,1)$, $f_X(t)=2(1-t)$ and $f_Y(t)=2t$, zero elsewhere. What is $\mathbb{P}(X\le1/4)$, the lower-tail area used in their crossing comparison?
On $(0,1)$, $f_X(t)=2(1-t)$ and $f_Y(t)=2t$, with CDFs $F_X(t)=2t-t^2$ and $F_Y(t)=t^2$. At $t=3/4$, what are the signs of density difference and CDF difference?
options: Density gap negative; CDF gap positive.
Density gap negative; CDF gap negative.
Density gap positive; CDF gap positive.
Density gap positive; CDF gap negative.

questions.question: Discrete loss $X$ is 0 or 2 with probabilities $0.7,0.3$; $Y$ is 1 or 3 with the same probabilities. Their CDFs are $F_X,F_Y$. Which cumulative comparison gives their stochastic order?
options: $F_X(t)\le F_Y(t)$ for every t.
$F_X(t)=F_Y(t)$ for every t.
$F_X(t)\ge F_Y(t)$ for every t.
The CDF order cannot be assessed without densities.

questions.question: $X$ has density $1/2$ on $(0,2)$. $Y$ has density $3/4$ on $(0,1/2)\cup(3/2,2)$ and $1/4$ on $(1/2,3/2)$; both are zero elsewhere. Their densities are symmetric about 1. Which mean pair supports the two-crossing thicker-tail criterion?
options: X has mean 1; Y has mean 3/2.
X has mean 1; Y has mean 1/2.
Both means equal 2.
Both means equal 1.

questions.question: Two normalised absolutely continuous densities intersect once. An analyst concludes $X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y$ merely from the number of intersections. What further information is needed?
options: Equality of both density heights at every point.
The direction of the signed density difference.
Independence of X and Y under one joint law.
Equality of both loss means in every comparison.

questions.question: Normalised densities have $f_Y-f_X$ non-negative, then non-positive, then non-negative on three consecutive intervals. An analyst wants to infer that Y is directly thicker-tailed than X. Which additional premise belongs to this criterion?
options: Their finite means must be equal.
Their means must be ordered strictly upwards.
Their CDFs must be ordered in one direction everywhere.
Their random variables must have independent realisations.

questions.question: For two normalised equal-mean densities, $f_Y-f_X$ has signs positive, negative, positive on three regions. Does the CDF crossing have to occur at one of the two density crossings?
options: Yes; integrating leaves every crossing point fixed.
Yes; the first density crossing is always the CDF crossing.
Yes; the second density crossing is always the CDF crossing.
No; the cumulative gap depends on integrated signed areas.

questions.question: $X$ has density $1/2$ on $(0,2)$. $Y$ has density $3/4$ on $(0,1/2)\cup(3/2,2)$ and $1/4$ on $(1/2,3/2)$, both zero elsewhere. Where in the middle interval does $F_Y-F_X$ change sign?

Densities $f_X(t)=2(1-t)$ and $f_Y(t)=2t$ on $(0,1)$ cross at $1/2$ and give $X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y$. Define translated losses $A=X+5$ and $B=Y+5$. Which threshold and comparison apply to the translated densities?
options: Threshold 5.5; A is stochastically no larger than B.
Threshold 0.5; A is stochastically no larger than B.
Threshold 5.5; B is stochastically no larger than A.
Threshold 5.5; the translated CDF gap changes sign.

questions.question: Two normalised densities are zero above 4, and their difference $f_X-f_Y$ equals $-1/5$ throughout $(3,4)$. What is $F_X(7/2)-F_Y(7/2)$, determined from the remaining tail?

On unit intervals $(0,1),(1,2),(2,3),(3,4)$, density $f_X$ is respectively $0.35,0.20,0.35,0.10$, while $f_Y=0.25$ throughout $(0,4)$; both vanish elsewhere. Does the three-sign-change density difference prevent $X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y$?
options: Yes; stochastic order requires exactly one density crossing.
Yes; the negative second interval forces a negative CDF gap.
No; its cumulative gap remains non-negative.
No; the smaller mean of X alone establishes the order.

questions.question: Two absolutely continuous losses have equal finite means. Their normalised density difference $f_X-f_Y$ is non-negative then non-positive and is strictly positive on an interval. Can all these premises hold simultaneously?
options: No; the inferred stochastic order and equal means force equal laws.
Yes; equal means never constrain a CDF ordering.
Yes; every strict density gap disappears after integration.
No; a stochastic comparison requires independent losses.

questions.question: $X$ is uniform on $(0,2)$. For $p\in(1/4,3/4)$, $Y$ has density $2p$ on $(0,1/2)$, zero on $(1/2,3/2)$ and $2(1-p)$ on $(3/2,2)$. All other values have density zero. Which p permits the equal-mean two-crossing criterion to conclude Y is directly thicker-tailed?
options: Every p in the stated interval.

questions.question: $X=1$ surely; $Y$ equals 0 or 2 with equal probabilities. Both means are 1. Their CDF difference $F_Y-F_X$ is positive below 1 and negative at 1. Which crossing convention correctly describes this direct thicker-tail comparison?
options: Both sides include 1 and demand equality there.
Lower side t<1; upper side t≥1.
Lower side t≤1; upper side t>1.
Discard the point t=1 as a density-version choice.
